metadata.description: Documented Gojri grammatical rules based on published linguistic field studies and grammars.
references: Sharma, J. C. (1982). Gojri Grammar. CIIL Mysore.
Losey, Wayne E. (2002). Writing Gojri. SIL International / University of North Dakota.
Grierson, George A. (1908). Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX, Part IV.

rules.name: Retroflex Consonant Inventory and Tonal Genesis
rules.description: Gojri features a complete retroflex stop series (/ṭ/, /ṭh/, /ḍ/, /ḍh/) alongside retroflex nasal /ṇ/ and flap /ṛ/. Historical loss of voiced aspirates or glottal friction in intervocalic/final positions frequently conditions pitch-accent or tonal contours on adjoining vowels.

examples.translation_en: horse (voiced velar aspirate /gh/ with retroflex flap /ṛ/)

rules.name: Masculine Marked Nouns in -o / -aa
rules.description: Marked masculine nouns end in /-o/ (or /-ā/ in eastern dialect variants). In the direct plural and oblique singular, the final /-o/ shifts to /-e/. In the oblique plural, it takes /-yā̃/ or /-ā̃/.

examples.gojri: گھوڑو (واحد مستقیم) -> گھوڑے (جمع مستقیم / واحد مائل) -> گھوڑیاں (جمع مائل)

rules.name: Feminine Marked Nouns in -i
rules.description: Feminine nouns commonly end in /-i/. The plural is formed by adding /-yā̃/ or /-ā̃/ in both direct and oblique cases.

rules.name: Personal Pronoun Case Alternation
rules.description: First and second person pronouns have distinct direct and oblique/agentive forms. When followed by postpositions (e.g., dative nā / accusative / agentive ne), first-person singular shifts to man- / maĩ-.

rules.name: Split-Ergative Case Marking with 'ne'
rules.description: Gojri operates a split-ergative alignment in the perfective (past completed) aspect with transitive verbs. The agent subject takes the postposition 'ne' (transcribed 'nE' by Sharma), while the verb agrees in gender and number with the direct object patient.

examples.translation_en: The boy ate bread (bread is feminine, verb khādī agrees with roṭī).
The girl ate a mango (mango is masculine, verb khāyo agrees with ām).

rules.name: Genitive Marker Concord (ro / ra / ri / re)
rules.description: The genitive postposition inflects like an adjective, agreeing with the head noun in gender, number, and case: 'ro' (m.sg.dir), 'ra' or 're' (m.pl.dir / m.sg.obl), 'ri' (f.sg/pl).

rules.name: Infinitive Suffix in -ṇo / -no
rules.description: The citation / infinitive form of Gojri verbs is formed by appending /-ṇo/ (after vowels, retroflexes, and liquids) or /-no/ (after dentals/nasals) to the verbal root.

rules.name: Habitual / Imperfective Aspect in -to / -ti
rules.description: The present habitual/imperfective aspect is marked on the verbal root with the suffix /-to/ (m.sg), /-te/ (m.pl), /-ti/ (f.sg), /-tiyā̃/ (f.pl), followed by present copula auxiliaries.

rules.name: Future Tense Marking in -go / -ga / -gi
rules.description: The future tense is expressed by suffixing /-go/ (masculine singular), /-ga/ (masculine plural), and /-gi/ (feminine) to the inflected subjunctive verb base.

rules.name: Pre-verbal Negation Particles ('na', 'nahī̃')
rules.description: Negation in indicative clauses is formed by placing 'nahī̃' or 'na' immediately before the main verb or auxiliary. Imperative / prohibitive negation uses 'mat' or 'na'.

rules.name: Canonical SOV Word Order
rules.description: Standard sentence structure in Gojri follows Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) order. Adverbs typically precede verbs, and modifiers precede head nouns.

examples.gojri: چھورو [S] گھوڑے ناں [O] گھاہ [O2] دیوے ہے [V]
examples.roman: chhoro [S] ghoṛe nā [O] ghāh [O2] dīve hai [V]
examples.translation_en: The boy gives grass to the horse.

rules.name: East vs. West Gojri Nominal and Genitive Differences
rules.description: Western Gojri (Hazara, Swat, Muzaffarabad) shows heavier Punjabi/Pahari phonetic influence, while Eastern and Jammu Gojri retains archaic Rajasthani traits such as genitive 'ro/ri' and masculine endings in '-o'.

examples.gojri: جموں / پونچھ: گھوڑو، اس رو | مغربی ہزارہ: گھوڑا، اس دا
examples.roman: Jammu/Poonch: ghoṛo, us ro | Western/Hazara: ghoṛā, us dā
examples.translation_en: horse / of him (contrasting genitive ro vs dā)

rules.name: Echo-Word Formation with /v-/ Replacement
rules.description: Gojri features productive expressives and echo-formations to signify 'X and related items/activities'. If the base begins with a consonant other than /v-/, the initial consonant is replaced with /v-/ (e.g. kām -> kām-vām, chāh -> chāh-vāh). If the base begins with /p-/, it often alternates with /dh-/ (e.g. pāṇi -> pāṇi-dhāṇi).

rules.name: Interrogative Particles and Question Formation
rules.description: Wh-questions employ dedicated question pronouns placed in pre-verbal focus: 'ke / kai' (what), 'koṇ' (who), 'kiddhar / kithe' (where), 'kadoñ / kad' (when), 'kyon' (why), and 'kiso' (what kind of). Polar (yes/no) questions employ rising intonation or sentence-initial 'ke'.

rules.name: Imperative and Prohibitive Verb Inflection
rules.description: Imperative forms vary by degree of honorificity and number. Informal singular commands use the bare verb root (e.g. bol! 'speak!'). Plural and polite commands suffix /-o/ (e.g. bolo! 'speak!'). Prohibitive (negative commands) place 'mat' or 'na' before the verb.

rules.name: Adjectival and Head-Noun Concord
rules.description: Marked adjectives in /-o/ systematically agree with head nouns in gender, number, and case: masculine singular direct takes /-o/ (chaṅgo), masculine plural and masculine oblique takes /-e/ (chaṅge), and feminine takes /-i/ (chaṅgi).

rules.name: Nominal Derivation via Suffixation (-āī, -vālo)
rules.description: Productive derivational suffixes include /-āī/ to form abstract qualities from adjectives (chaṅgo -> chaṅgāī 'goodness', mīṭho -> miṭhāī 'sweetness') and /-vālo/ to denote agent, possessor, or practitioner (ghoṛewālo 'horse-keeper', ḍerewālo 'camp-dweller').

examples.translation_en: camp -> person of the camp / nomadic herdsman

rules.name: Subordination and Relative-Correlative Clauses
rules.description: Complex sentences use relative-correlative pairs: 'je ... te ...' (if ... then ... conditional) or 'jo ... so ...' (whoever ... he ... relative). Complement clauses are introduced by the complementizer 'ke' or 'ki' positioned between matrix and subordinate verbs.

examples.gojri: جے توں آواں گو تے اسی ملساں
examples.roman: je tū̃ āvā̃ go te asī̃ milsā̃
examples.translation_en: If you come, then we will meet.

rules.name: Ergative Pronoun Case Alternations
rules.description: First and second person personal pronouns in Gojri display distinct ergative/agentive forms in perfective transitive constructions: mẽ (1st sg. by me), tẽ (2nd sg. by you), asā̃ (1st pl. by us), tusā̃ (2nd pl. by you). The overt postposition ne is primarily employed with 3rd person demonstratives/nouns (us ne, chhore ne).

examples.translation_en: You wrote a letter (ergative 2nd person tẽ).
He saw the horse (3rd person pronoun with ne).

rules.name: Comparative and Superlative Formations with Ablative Markers
rules.description: Comparison of adjectives is achieved syntactically rather than through inflectional suffixes. The standard of comparison is marked with the ablative postposition thā̃ (or kolū̃ / nalū̃), followed by the base adjective. Superlative meaning is formed using saglā̃ thā̃ (than all) or sab thā̃.

examples.gojri: ایہہ گھوڑو اس تھوں چنگو ہے
examples.roman: eh ghoṛo us thā̃ chaṅgo hai
examples.translation_en: This horse is better than that one (Comparative with thā̃).
He is the biggest/eldest of all (Superlative with saglā̃ thā̃).
